title: CPU, memory and disk investigation
description: Diagnose CPU, memory, and disk bottlenecks on production Linux servers.

data.text: Production servers have limited CPU, memory, and disk. When any of these resources becomes scarce, applications slow down or crash. The skill is not just reading numbers: it is knowing which numbers matter, what normal looks like, and how to trace a bottleneck back to a specific process or query.

CPU, memory, and disk are interconnected. A process that is CPU-bound may not be using much memory. A process that leaks memory can trigger disk thrashing when the system starts swapping. By understanding each resource, you can build a mental model of why the system is stressed.

CPU is measured in cores and utilization percentage. A single-threaded process can only use one core at a time, so 100% CPU for that process equals one full core. Multi-threaded applications can use multiple cores. High CPU means the system is doing a lot of computation. Low CPU does not mean the system is healthy: it could mean it is waiting on I/O.

The top command shows CPU usage by process. The mpstat command breaks CPU usage by core. The uptime command gives a one-minute load average. Load average is the average number of processes waiting to run. If load average exceeds the number of cores, the system is overloaded.

data.code:
top -bn1 | head -20
mpstat -P ALL 1 5
uptime
# Check which process is using CPU
pidstat -u 1 5

data.text: Linux memory is divided into RAM and swap. RAM is fast; swap is disk-based and slow. The free command shows total, used, free, and available memory. Available memory is more useful than free because it includes memory that can be reclaimed from caches.

A process can use memory in many ways: stack, heap, code segments, shared libraries, and memory-mapped files. The VIRT column in top shows virtual memory size, which includes all of these. The RES column shows resident set size, which is the actual physical memory the process is using. RES is usually the number you care about.

data.code:
free -h
vmstat 1 10
# Check memory per process
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -10

data.title: OOM killer
data.text: When the system runs out of memory, the kernel activates the OOM (Out of Memory) killer. It selects a process and kills it to free memory. Check dmesg or /var/log/syslog for OOM events. The killed process is usually the one using the most memory, but not always the one you expect.

Disk issues come in two flavors: running out of space and slow disk performance. The df command shows space usage by filesystem. The du command shows space usage by directory. The iostat command shows disk I/O throughput and latency.

items: df -h: shows disk usage and mount points
du -sh /path/*: shows which directories use the most space
iostat -x 1: shows I/O utilization and latency per device

data.code:
df -h
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -rh | head -10
iostat -x 1 5
# Find large files
find / -size +100M -exec ls -lh {} \;

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: Load average above core count means the CPU queue is too long
RES memory is the actual physical memory a process uses
Swap is a safety net, not a performance feature
OOM killer kills processes when memory is exhausted
Use du and iostat to find disk space and I/O bottlenecks
